name: Ribeye and water carnivore

lead: Ribeye and water is shorthand for a very narrow carnivore diet where fatty beef steak is the main or only food. People use it to take decisions out of eating, aiming for leanness, muscle and clearer skin.

The chain is that a fatty, protein-rich steak is filling and the menu is so limited that intake stays simple and predictable. Carnivore advocates recommend fatty cuts such as ribeye, 80/20 ground beef and added tallow so most calories come from fat. It is not a separately studied protocol; the research that exists covers the wider carnivore diet and is mostly self-reports.

paras: Meals are steak, sometimes with ground beef or tallow, and water. People typically use it as a short, strict stretch or a base for broader carnivore eating, and report on appetite and digestion within the first weeks.
Concerns raised for the wider carnivore diet include fibre and micronutrient gaps, a documented scurvy case on mostly canned beef, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation, gout and kidney strain.

angle.text: Followers cut eating down to fatty beef and water so meals stay filling and simple, aiming for a leaner body, muscle and clearer skin. It is an informal shorthand within carnivore eating, and studies cover the wider carnivore diet rather than this version.

lead: Ribeye and water is shorthand for an extremely narrow carnivore diet built around fatty beef steaks and water. Adherents follow it as a stripped-down elimination approach, commonly with goals such as a leaner physique and a simpler routine, since all food decisions reduce to one cut of beef.[1][2]

Grokipedia does not describe it as a distinct named protocol, but notes that carnivore advocates recommend fatty cuts such as ribeye, 80/20 ground beef and added tallow so that most calories come from fat rather than protein.[2] It sits within the carnivore diet family, which allows only animal foods; the closest named variants on Wikipedia are the "lion diet" (beef only, followed in a version with salt and water by Mikhaila and Jordan Peterson) and the historical Salisbury meat and hot water diet.[1]

Evidence for the family consists mainly of self-reports; the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia classify the diet as a fad diet.[1] No published study has tested a ribeye-only pattern.
infobox: Shawn Baker, Mikhaila and Jordan Peterson[1]

paras: Carnivore advocates favour fatty cuts of ruminant meat to supply most energy as fat, since very lean meat without enough fat can cause fatigue, nausea and diarrhoea, a condition Grokipedia calls protein poisoning or rabbit starvation.[2] The ribeye-and-water pattern reduces variety to a minimum, which proponents present as a simple elimination approach.

Wikipedia dates precursors of meat-centred diets to the nineteenth century: Bernard Moncriff's 1856 book, Arnaldo Cantani's animal-based diet for diabetic patients in the 1870s, and James H. Salisbury's 1880s regimen of lean beef and hot water for several weeks.[1] The modern carnivore diet was promoted from 2018 by Shawn Baker, a former orthopaedic surgeon, who wrote a book on it; the lion diet later spread on TikTok.[1] Vilhjalmur Stefansson's 1928 supervised meat-only year is also cited as a precedent.[2]

Wikipedia lists missing fibre, vitamin deficiencies, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation, possible kidney strain, and colon cancer and gout risk with high red-meat intake as concerns, and states that nutrition scientists regard it as an extreme fad diet.[1] Grokipedia adds scurvy, kidney-stone and bone concerns and notes that health bodies generally advise against long-term adherence.[2]
No studies found. A 2021 survey of carnivore dieters described by Grokipedia reported high self-rated improvement, but it was self-selected and did not test a ribeye-only pattern.[2]

timeline.event: Bernard Moncriff publishes The Philosophy of the Stomach and reportedly lives on beef and milk for a year.[1]
James H. Salisbury promotes a lean beef and hot water diet.[1]
Vilhjalmur Stefansson completes a supervised meat-only year.[2]
Shawn Baker promotes the carnivore diet on social media.[1]
